report.answer_text:
Solar Orbiter captured the first clear images of the Sun’s south pole in March 2025. Its magnetic maps revealed patches of both north and south magnetic polarity side by side, rather than one dominant polarity. ESA released the images on June 11, 2025. (esa.int)
That patchwork is characteristic of solar maximum, the active phase of the Sun’s roughly 11-year cycle when its global magnetic field reverses. (esa.int)

quotes.text: The Spectral Imaging of the Coronal Environment (SPICE) instrument on the ESA-led Solar Orbiter spacecraft got its first good look at the Sun's south pole in March 2025.
The collage above shows the Sun’s south pole as recorded on 16–17 March 2025, when Solar Orbiter was viewing the Sun from an angle of 15° below the solar equator.

quotes.text: These groundbreaking new observations are also key to understanding the Sun’s magnetic field and why it flips roughly every 11 years, coinciding with a peak in solar activity.
This happens only for a short time during each solar cycle, at solar maximum, when the Sun’s magnetic field flips and is at its most active.

pages.quote_reason: The quotes state that at solar maximum, the peak-activity point of the roughly 11-year cycle, the Sun's magnetic field flips and is at its most active, which covers every fact in the claim.
